Where it began

Madan Lal Udhouram Sharma was born in Amritsar on 20 March 1951. He began with Punjab and later moved to Delhi, and in domestic cricket he was a serious all-rounder by any measure. In first-class matches he scored 10,204 runs at 42.87 with 22 hundreds, and took 625 wickets at 25.50. Few players carry both loads so well for so long.

The player

He played 39 Tests for India from 1974 to 1986, making 1,042 runs with five fifties and a best of 74, and taking 71 wickets with a best of 5 for 23. He bowled with a side-on action, the kind coaches like to show in a textbook.

The one-day game gave him his most famous days. At the 1975 World Cup he bowled the first ball to England's Dennis Amiss. Eight years later he was part of the attack that strangled the opposition in the 1983 final at Lord's, sharing the work with Kapil Dev, Roger Binny, Balwinder Sandhu, Kirti Azad and Mohinder Amarnath. It was off his bowling that Kapil Dev took the extraordinary catch that sent back Vivian Richards. Two years on he was in the India squad that won the World Championship of Cricket in 1985. In all he played 67 one-day internationals.

What made him special

He was a fighter with the bat in the lower order. So often did he dig India out of awkward spots that grateful fans nicknamed him Maddad Lal. That is a better nickname than most cricketers ever earn.

If Test cricket was a little less kind to his bowling than the domestic game had been, with 40.08 runs for each of his wickets, he never stopped running in, and his four five-wicket innings showed what he could do when the ball moved.

Away from the middle

He received the Arjuna Award. After playing he gave a great deal back as a coach. He took charge of the United Arab Emirates at the 1996 World Cup and was India's national coach from September 1996 to September 1997. He later sat on the national selection committee, coached the Delhi Giants, had his own academy at Delhi's Siri Fort Sports Complex, and in 2010 was appointed to lead the coaching at the Sanjay Jagdale MPCA Academy.

And finally

When the film 83 told the story of that World Cup win in 2021, Harrdy Sandhu played Madan Lal. Not many bowlers get to see themselves on the big screen, and fewer get to watch their most important ball caught all over again in cinemas.
